analysis.one_liner: Restricts high-cost mortgages, banning abusive fees, flipping, and mandatory arbitration.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a House vote: after being referred to the Financial Services Committee and two subcommittees in 2005, it died when the 109th Congress ended in January 2007.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have placed federal restrictions on high-cost mortgages — loans with rates or fees well above the market norm. It would have banned lenders from making loans borrowers cannot repay, blocking most prepayment penalties and balloon payments, outlawing single-premium credit insurance and mandatory arbitration clauses, requiring counseling before a high-cost loan, and letting borrowers sue for three years after a violation. It never advanced past committee.
analysis.who_benefits: Homeowners and buyers taking out high-cost or subprime mortgages — disproportionately lower-income and minority borrowers — would get protection from loans structured to strip home equity: no lending without regard to ability to repay, capped late fees, no balloon payments, no single-premium credit insurance rolled into the loan, no mandatory arbitration, and longer windows to sue over violations.

how_it_helps.text: Requires that a lender reasonably believe the borrower can make the payments, based on income and debts rather than home equity, with a presumption of violation for a pattern of undocumented loans [S3].
Prohibits flipping — refinancing a mortgage that brings the borrower no reasonable, tangible net benefit — and bans lenders from recommending default before a refinancing [S2, S3].
Bans single-premium credit insurance financing in all home-secured loans and prohibits mandatory arbitration clauses, preserving the borrower's right to sue in court [S2, S3].

Caps late fees, restricts prepayment penalties and balloon payments, outlaws most modification and payoff-statement fees, requires HUD-approved pre-loan counseling, and extends the statute of limitations for violations to three years while doubling civil penalties [S2, S3].

analysis.who_pays: High-cost mortgage lenders and mortgage brokers, who would lose fee income, prepayment penalties, single-premium insurance commissions, and the ability to structure loans around the restrictions; credit insurers selling single-premium policies would lose that sales channel.

drawbacks.text: Mandatory pre-loan counseling adds a required step — and delay — before any high-cost loan can close, including for borrowers who understand the terms and want the money quickly [S3].

An honest supporter would acknowledge that tighter underwriting and fee caps reduce the supply of credit to borrowers with damaged finances, who turn to high-cost lenders precisely because mainstream lenders will not serve them [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The protections target practices — equity stripping, loans made without regard to repayment, hidden fee stacking — whose costs fall on the borrowers least able to bear them. The counseling mandate and reduced credit availability for marginal borrowers are real costs, but the bill preserves conventional prepayment penalties for near-market-rate loans and lets consumers choose counseling-verified loans, so the design tries to spare ordinary mortgage lending.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Financial Services Committee, then to two subcommittees, and sat there until the Congress ended two years later without ever reaching the House floor.

narrative.text: Representative Brad Miller of North Carolina introduced the bill on March 9, 2005, joined by Representatives Mel Watt and Barney Frank [S3].
It was referred to the House Committee on Financial Services the day it was introduced [S5].
On May 13, 2005, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Financial Institutions and Consumer Credit and the Subcommittee on Housing and Community Opportunity — where action stalled [S5].
No further action appears in the record; the bill died when the 109th Congress ended on January 3, 2007 [S1, S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: High-cost mortgage lenders and brokers were better off, because they kept operating without the federal restrictions on fees, flipping, and arbitration the bill would have imposed. Borrowers gained nothing from the outcome.

sides.party_line_note: All 67 cosponsors were Democrats or the chamber's Independent; the bill sat in committee under Republican control of the House and never came to a vote, so the outcome split along party control even though no roll call occurred [S4, S5].

industries.note: The bill would cap and count the points and fees these lenders charge, restrict prepayment penalties and balloon payments, require verified ability to repay, and ban flipping — eliminating the fee-stacking and equity-stripping practices their high-margin business relied on [S3].

The bill bans financing single-premium credit life, disability, unemployment, and property insurance in home-secured loans, removing a product sold upfront into the loan balance at high cost to borrowers [S3].
The bill makes pre-loan counseling by an independent, HUD-approved counselor a prerequisite for any high-cost mortgage, creating a mandated role for counseling agencies [S3].
